claims.text: A value object has no id of its own, so nothing in it can serve as its own key. In Đơn Hàng, Vnd holds a single value and is mapped with a value converter into its owner's row: no table or key of its own; its amount is a column of order_items.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang @ stage-3 DonHangDbContext.cs:80-96; EF Core docs: Value Conversions (Simple value objects)

claims.text: HasConversion(convertToProviderExpression, convertFromProviderExpression): EF Core applies the first expression when writing the property's value to the database and the second when reading the column value back into the property's type.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Value Conversions (Configuring a value converter; HasConversion with two expressions)

claims.text: The column type follows the converter's provider type, not the model type. With provider type int, EF Core with Npgsql maps the property to integer, as for an int property; the stage-3 snapshot records b.Property<int>("UnitPrice").HasColumnType("integer").
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Value Conversions (model/provider type); Npgsql EF Core type mapping (int -> integer); DonHangDbContextModelSnapshot.cs:123-125 @ stage-3

claims.text: The from-provider expression amount => new Vnd(amount) calls Vnd's constructor on every load, so a negative value in unit_price_vnd makes loading that row throw an exception instead of returning an item.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Value Conversions (conversion applied when reading); examples/don-hang @ stage-3: DonHangDbContext.cs:95, Vnd.cs:12-16

claims.text: Loading an Order through EF Core uses its private parameterless constructor, which checks nothing (contrast with Vnd, whose checking constructor the converter calls).
claims.source_hint: prereq design.l2.ef-core-and-private-setters summary lines 3-4; examples/don-hang @ stage-3: DonHang.Domain/Entities.cs (Order private constructor)

claims.text: At stage-3, DonHangDbContext maps OrderItem.UnitPrice with HasColumnName("unit_price_vnd").HasConversion(price => price.Amount, amount => new Vnd(amount)); there is no Entity<Vnd>, DbSet<Vnd>, HasKey or ToTable for Vnd. At stage-2 (line 75) the int UnitPriceVnd mapped to the same column name.
In OnModelCreating, Entity<T>() configures entity type T, ToTable sets its table name and HasKey configures its primary key (several properties give a composite key).
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Entity Types (Table name); Keys (configuring a primary key, composite keys)

claims.text: At stage-3, OrderItemDto is record OrderItemDto(int ProductId, int Quantity, int UnitPriceVnd), and OrdersController builds it with new OrderItemDto(i.ProductId, i.Quantity, i.UnitPrice.Amount).
ASP.NET Core's default JSON options serialize an int property UnitPriceVnd as a JSON number under the camelCase name unitPriceVnd; the stage-3 capture shows "unitPriceVnd":450000.
claims.source_hint: ASP.NET Core docs: Format response data (System.Text.Json, camelCase default); examples/don-hang outputs/stage-3/scripts/backend/auth-and-orders.txt:8

claims.text: At stage-3, DonHang.App's models.dart reads an order item's price with json['unitPriceVnd'] as int.
When EF Core maps a property of type Vnd with a value converter, it treats it as a scalar property stored in one column and adds no entity type for Vnd to the model.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Value Conversions (Simple value objects); execution: Model.FindEntityType(typeof(Vnd)) is null

claims.text: Changing unitPriceVnd to an object would break a client that reads it as a number, such as DonHang.App; while Đơn Hàng has one currency, an object with a currency field adds no check the domain lacks. Opposing view: a structured money object is right when the API must carry several currencies.
